passage: My name is Charu, and for months I believed something about me made people want to tease me. The girls behind me in class copied how I spoke and giggled, so I started sitting very straight and saying nothing. At home I kept my face bright so Mummy would not ask. One evening I dropped a glass and cried far too hard, and Mummy sat down beside me on the kitchen floor. It all came out. She said the girls' cruelty came from something in them, not from a flaw in me. I still felt shy afterwards, but Mummy and Lavanya Ma'am, my class teacher, made a plan, and the weight in my chest felt smaller.

qa.q: What did the girls behind Charu do in class?
qa.a: They copied how Charu spoke and giggled.

qa.q: How did Charu feel about the teasing before she told Mummy?
qa.a: Charu felt ashamed and worried, believing something about her made people tease her, so she sat very straight, said nothing and kept her face bright at home.

qa.q: How did Charu's mother respond in a way that eased the blame Charu had been carrying?
qa.a: Mummy listened first and said the cruelty came from the girls, not from a flaw in Charu, and then worked with the class teacher on a plan.

qa.q: How might Lavanya Ma'am see the situation when Mummy comes to talk?
qa.a: Lavanya Ma'am probably learns something that had not been noticed in class and can now watch more closely and support Charu.

grounding: A child blames themself for being picked on, then shares it with Mummy and a teacher and feels lighter.

passage:
Rekha's school pinafore had been her cousin's, and its hem was let down twice. A group of girls in her class called her "hand-me-down" and held their noses when she passed. Rekha started to believe there was something wrong with her. At night she tried to scrub the faded patch white.
Her father, Darshan, drove an auto and worked late, so she barely saw him. On his only day off she was ironing the pinafore when he asked, "Why so quiet, beti?"
She told him everything. He switched off the iron and held her. "This is not your fault. Those girls are the problem, not you." Together they walked to the school that afternoon to meet the class teacher.

qa.q: Whose pinafore had Rekha's school pinafore been before?
Why did Rekha scrub the faded patch at night?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and believed something must be wrong with her, as if fixing the pinafore could stop the teasing.

qa.q: What did Darshan do that lifted the weight Rekha was carrying?
qa.a: He stopped ironing, held her, told her it was not her fault, and went with her to the class teacher that same afternoon.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel when he hears about the teasing?
qa.a: He may feel protective and sad that she carried it alone while he worked late, which is why he acts that very afternoon.

grounding: A girl picked on for her hand-me-down uniform believes something is wrong with her; her father says it is not her fault and they go to the teacher together.

passage:
Jasleen was the tallest girl in Class 6 at her Delhi school, and three boys had started calling her "lamp post" and ducking when she walked by. She began to slouch everywhere, even at home. Maybe being tall was a bad thing, she thought. Maybe she was the problem.
After maths she stayed behind. "Avni Ma'am, can I tell you something?" Her voice shook.
Avni Ma'am put down her marker and listened. "It is not your fault, Jasleen. People who pick on others are usually dealing with something of their own. You were right to tell me." She spoke to the boys' class teacher at break that same day. Jasleen walked home standing a little straighter.

qa.q: What did the three boys call Jasleen?
What does Jasleen's slouching suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt ashamed of her height and had started to believe she was the problem.

qa.q: What made Avni Ma'am's response helpful?
qa.a: She stopped, listened, told Jasleen it was not her fault, and took action with the boys' class teacher the same day.

qa.q: How might Avni Ma'am see Jasleen's decision to stay behind?
qa.a: Avni Ma'am sees it as brave and right, telling Jasleen she was right to speak up.

grounding: A tall girl picked on by boys comes to believe she is the problem; telling her teacher, who says it is not her fault and acts, lifts the weight.
